head: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution Jiawei Zhou1,2 Bo Peng1,3 Yuxuan Huang1,3 Ming Zhang1 Youbang Sun1,5* Xiang Wang1,4 Chaochao Lu1* 1Shanghai AI Laboratory 2Fudan University 3Shanghai Jiao Tong University 4University of Science and Technology of China 5Tsinghua University Abstract Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, by rewriting its skill, a natural-language proce- dure in its context, and keeping the edits that raise success on a small dev set. On such tasks success is noisy, so a gain on a small dev set does not show that an edit helps, and a success score does not show what the edit costs. We introduce BiPA, which replays an optimizer’s acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read to trace extra input tokens to the behavior behind them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks and two models, the learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seed, 0.1 points higher on average. Their dev gains vanish on test: keeping the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when none changed. They read about 16% more input tokens: the optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them

Built for soft- ware engineering, these harnesses now run agents on other long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a ter- minal environment, serving a customer or running a *Corresponding authors. business workflow. An agent is adapted to a family of such tasks with a skill, a natural-language proce- dure that the harness places in the model’s context at the start of every task. Skill optimizers auto- mate this, starting from a seed skill (Agrawal et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026): an editor model reads the trajectories, the logs of the agent’s runs on training tasks, and turns their successes and failures into rules, and a gate keeps an edit if the agent with the edited skill solves more tasks of a small development set, the dev set. These optimiz- ers report gains, mostly on short, cheap tasks such as question answering, and controlled studies find the gains sparse and fragile (Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). We introduce BiPA, which replays an optimizer’s acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read to trace extra input tokens to the behavior behind them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks and two models, the learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seed, 0.1 points higher on average. Their dev gains vanish on test: keeping the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when none changed. They read about 16% more input tokens: the optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them as extra turns, each re-sending the whole conversation. Four principles follow: accept an edit only if its gain exceeds what se- lection alone reports; charge it for the turns it adds, not for its length; let the editor delete and merge rules; show it what earlier rules cost.
